reason: CUTGUARD v2 G4. Rule 3 refuses an ownership id sourced from a fetched row instead of the session — the shape that made POST /scheduled-rides/:id/conflict-acknowledge a check that could not fail, live on the pilot. Every entry below was read at abb6a26 and each names what DOES authorise its call: an entry that only says 'this is fine' is not an attestation. Two categories recur and both are real: an ENTITY REFERENCE (a row's own primary key handed to the function that updates that row — not an authorisation at all, and the authorisation stands separately above it), and NO SESSION EXISTS (a gateway webhook, authorised by the processor's own reference rather than by a user). A site that is neither belongs in code, not here.

ENTITY REFERENCE, and the ownership check is done correctly one line above. Both handlers fetch the escrow by the id in the body and then compare `escrow.customerId !== req.user!.userId` → 403 FORBIDDEN — against the SESSION, which is exactly what conflict-acknowledge failed to do. `escrow.id` is then the row to mark, not a claim about who is asking.
ENTITY REFERENCE. Same two handlers and the same session-sourced `escrow.customerId !== req.user!.userId` → 403 above it; this is the failure arm of the same charge.

A ROUND-TRIP, not a tautology. `user` is fetched as `prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: req.user!.userId } })`, so `user.id` IS the session id — it came from req.user and went back. Behind authMiddleware + driverOnly + requireMoneyStepUp. Passing req.user!.userId directly would read better and change nothing; it is left as-is because this dispatch does not touch payout handlers it has no defect in.

Same round-trip as the sibling above: `user` is fetched by `where: { id: req.user!.userId }`, so `user.id` is the session id. Behind authMiddleware + driverOnly + requireMoneyStepUp, and firePreferenceChangeBatch carries the freeze, AML hard-cap, in-flight-transfer and balance-floor guards itself.

NO SESSION EXISTS. This is Flutterwave's transfer.completed callback — there is no req.user to source anything from, and there never can be. The batch is resolved by the processor's own `data.reference` against the unique DriverPayoutBatch.txRef, and the driver it pays is whichever driver that batch is for; taking the driver from anywhere else would be the bug. Authorisation for the request itself is the webhook signature check, not a user.
NO SESSION EXISTS, and an ENTITY REFERENCE besides: the id of the batch resolved from the gateway's own txRef, handed to the function that settles that batch.
NO SESSION EXISTS. The failure arm of the same gateway callback, on the same txRef-resolved batch.
